fields.connection: ([scope]の中で) + Nが + いちばん + A/Na/V
examples: This movie is the most interesting.
Of spring, summer, fall, and winter, I like fall the best.
Tanaka is the tallest in the class.
This problem is the most difficult.
Among Japanese dishes, sushi is the most famous.
This is the store closest to the station.
fields.explain:
Marking the scope: Use ～の中で／～で to avoid ambiguity.
Topic vs. subject: both Nは/がいちばん～ are possible; は presents the topic, while が emphasizes identification: “N is the very one that is the most”.
In formal written language, consider 最も to avoid a colloquial tone.
Position: いちばん comes before adjectives/verbs of quality: いちばん大きい、いちばん好きだ.

Expresses the highest degree within a set/scope: “N is the most …”.
“いちばん” is an adverb of degree that modifies adjectives/stative verbs: いちばん新しい、いちばん好きだ.
Often used with a scope marked by ～の中で／～で to make the target of comparison clear.
Compared with 最も, いちばん has a casual nuance and is often used in conversation.
fields.notes:
“いちばん～ない” can be ambiguous; to express “the least/not the most …”, consider “最も～ではない/最も～とは言えない”.
“一番上/一番前/一番後ろ” are used to indicate position; this is still a usage of いちばん as an adverb of degree/position.
Sample question: “AとBとCで、どれがいちばん～ですか”。
mistakes: Omitting the scope makes the sentence needlessly absolute: “富士山がいちばん高い” → better to write “日本で、富士山が…”.
Confusing もっと (comparative) with いちばん (superlative).
Using は/が against the intended focus: “Aは/がいちばん～” shifts the focus; the JLPT often tests the nuance of は vs. が.
Choosing 最も in a spoken-language context, or the other way around, is a common trap.

rows: <ruby>最<rt>もっとも</rt></ruby>も<ruby>重要<rt>じゅうよう</rt></ruby>だ。
Kanji form of いちばん
Exactly the same meaning; common in writing.

examples: I want a new bag.
Right now I want free time more than money.
What do you want for your birthday?
Tanaka seems to want a car.
I don't want such an expensive watch.
When I was a child, I wanted a dog.
fields.explain:
Most natural only for the speaker's own desire; for other people, add そうだ／らしい to avoid imposing assumptions:彼は新しいPCがほしいらしい。
In polite requests: 〜がほしいのですが、ありますか (I'd like ~; do you have it?).
Not used with verbs (actions). To say you want to do V, use Vたい.
Compared with ください: ください asks someone else to give/do something; ほしいです expresses your own desire.

Expresses a desire to possess something material/a condition: “I want N”. Mainly used for the speaker's wishes.
You can ask about the listener's desire directly:何がほしいですか。
When talking about a third party's desire, use ほしがる/ほしがっている to stay objective and avoid subjective attribution.
Distinguish it from ください (asking for/requesting) and 欲しいのですが… (opening a polite request).
fields.notes:
Particle: が is usually used to emphasize what is wanted; を also occurs in spoken language when N is a specific target being taken/received: それをほしい (casual).
フォーマル:欲しております (humble/business) is rare and sounds stiff; it is usually replaced with ご希望です/ご入用です.
Avoid using it directly with superiors/customers: use いただけますでしょうか, 〜をお願いできますか instead.
explain: ほしい is an i-adjective.
examples: 1. A:　今　なにが　ほしいですか。
B:　カメラが　ほしいです。
A: What do you want now?
B: I want a camera.
2. 今　お金や車などがほしいですが、恋人がほしくないです。
Right now I want money, a car, and so on, but I don't want a partner.
mistakes: Using ほしい with verbs: incorrect. Correct: Vたい or 〜てほしい.
Stating a third party's desire with ほしいです: unnatural. Use ほしがる/ほしがっている/〜らしい.
Wrong particle: it must be Nがほしいです (in standard language). In spoken language you may hear Nをほしい, but it is not recommended on the exam.
Confusing the nuance of a request: “水がほしいです” only expresses a desire; to make a polite request, say “水をいただけますか”.

rows: For the speaker; OK when asking the listener
Expresses a wish for the target to carry out the action
Someone else seems to want N
Describes a third party, usually in ている
<ruby>子<rt>こ</rt></ruby>どもはお<ruby>菓<rt>かし</rt></ruby><ruby>子<rt></rt></ruby>をほしがっている

fields.connection: N (point in time: 3時・7月…) + ごろ
examples: I'll come by around 3 o'clock tomorrow.
I plan to go to Japan around July.
I was born around 1990.
It will probably start raining around evening.
I will arrive by around 8:30.
I've been busy lately and haven't been exercising.
fields.explain:
Neutral; used in both spoken and written language.
Used with “point” markers: hours, days, months, years, holidays; avoid attaching it to a “duration” such as 3時間 (3 hours is a length of time); if you mean “around 3 o'clock (a point)”, use 3時.
“このごろ/そのごろ/あのごろ” = “these days/at that time/in those days”.
When you need the nuance of a broad “period”, or with a past clause, prefer ころ over ごろ.

Indicates an approximate point in time: “around …” (3時ごろ = around 3 o'clock).
Flexibility: can take に (at), から (from), まで (until) to clarify the relationship.
Difference from ころ: ごろ usually attaches directly to a specific time marker; ころ leans toward a broad “period/span”, or follows a past clause.
fields.notes:
“このごろ” usually goes with the present/progressive; “その/あのころ” usually goes with the past.
“Nごろには” emphasizes “by around then …” (expecting a state at an approximate point).
Standard usage: “3時ごろに来てください” is more natural than “3時ころに…”, but both are accepted.
mistakes: Using it with a duration: “3時間ごろ” (incorrect); it should be “3時ごろ”.
Redundant double approximation: “3時ごろくらい／3時ごろぐらい” is incorrect; choose one.
Misreading deadlines: “5時ごろまでに提出” means “submit by around 5 o'clock” (an approximate point), unlike “5時までに” (an exact point).
Confusing ころ with ごろ: use ころ with a past clause/“the days of ~”:学生のころ(ごろ is not used).

rows: Attaches directly to a point in time
Used with Nの/ Vた + ころ; vaguer scope
<ruby>子<rt>こ</rt></ruby>どものころ／<ruby>帰<rt>かえ</rt></ruby>ったころ
Can be used with a point in time: <ruby>3時<rt>さんじ</rt></ruby>くらい; more colloquial than ごろ
<ruby>5時<rt>ごじ</rt></ruby>までに<ruby>提出<rt>ていしゅつ</rt></ruby>

fields.connection: N (person's name) + さん / ちゃん
examples: That person over there is Watt.

A: Is Thawaphon a student?
B: Yes, Thawaphon is a student.
fields.explain:
さん is used after the family name or given name of the listener or a third party. It is not used after your own family name or given name.
For children, ちゃん is used instead of さん, with a more casual nuance. ちゃん can be used for both boys and girls; there is no strict division with ちゃん for girls and くん for boys, as you may have learned before.

examples: You must not throw away trash here.
In Japan, you must not use words such as 「終わる」 or 「別れる」 in wedding speeches.
You must not ask people you've just met about their age or income.
You must not take photos here.
You must not make fun of people.
You must not break a promise.
fields.explain:
Used in rules/signs: ～てはいけません/～てはならない.
Used in everyday conversation: ～ちゃだめ／～ちゃいけない (soft or strong depending on the context and the listener).
When you need to be polite without being too harsh, you can use ～ないでください instead.
Absolute emphasis: ～てはならない (formal; authority/rules).

• Expresses prohibition: you are not allowed to do action V.
• The nuance ranges from neutral to strong depending on the variant; used in rules, regulations, and reminders.
• Different from the polite request “Please don't …” (～ないでください): ～てはいけない carries the meaning of prohibition/not permitting.
fields.notes:
• Unnatural when used to “ask for permission” (×「入っちゃいけませんか？」). To ask for permission, use ～てもいいですか。
• The negation of ～てはいけない is the affirmative “allowed” (→ ～てもいい), not “must do”.
• Negative form of the action before て: 飲まないではいけない means “must not drink” in the sense of “have to not drink”, which is completely different.
mistakes: Confusing it with ～ないといけない (must). The form looks similar because of “いけない”, but the meaning is the opposite.
Using ～てはならない in ordinary conversation → too stiff.
Forgetting は: ×「していけない」 → correct: してはいけない.
Choosing the wrong politeness level: with strangers, use ～てはいけません/～ないでください.

rows: <ruby>守<rt>まも</rt></ruby>らねばならない<ruby>規則<rt>きそく</rt></ruby>。
Polite request, milder than a prohibition.
ここで<ruby>話<rt>はな</rt></ruby>さないでください。
Different meaning (obligation); easy to confuse because of the form.
Moral/general evaluation, not an absolute prohibition.
<ruby>人<rt>ひと</rt></ruby>を<ruby>責<rt>せ</rt></ruby>めるべきではない。

examples: Which would you prefer, coffee or tea?
Which has higher prices, Tokyo or Osaka?
Which will you study, English or Chinese?
Which is faster, the bus or the train?
Which do you like better, the sea or the mountains? — I like the mountains better.
Which would you like, paper or plastic?
fields.explain:
More formal and polite than どっち. Suitable for written language and polite conversation.
Adding のほうが makes the answer natural: N1のほうが～です。
Emphasize contrast with ～とでは/～では right before どちら.
When asking about preferences/feelings, 好き/嫌い/得意/苦手 usually go with が.

This pattern is used to ask “between A and B, which one…?” when comparing two options.
と connects two parallel nouns; どちら is a question word meaning “which side/which one” (polite).
The particle after どちら depends on the predicate:
Adjective: どちらが高いですか。
Transitive verb: どちらを選びますか。
Location/destination: どちらにしますか。
Adjective: どちらが高いですか。
Transitive verb: どちらを選びますか。
Location/destination: どちらにしますか。
Extended forms: どちらのN (of which side), どちらのほう (which side more) to sound more natural when comparing degree.
fields.notes:
With nouns referring to people/companies, a 敬称 can be added, such as さん側/社: A社とB社とどちらが～。
Add ずっと/少し/やや before the adjective to quantify: どちらがずっと便利ですか。
どちら can be used for 2 directions/2 doors/2 places when asking for directions:右と左とどちらへ行きますか。
The answer can use 両方（both）
mistakes: Forgetting the second と: × AとBどちらが… → ○ AとBとどちらが…
Wrong particle after どちら: × どちらは好きですか → ○ どちらが好きですか。
Unnatural answer: × Aが好きです → ○ Aのほうが好きです (when comparing).
Using どれ for 2 specific options: use どちら/どっち.
JLPT trap: confusing どちらのN (of which side) with どちらが (subject of the comparison).

rows: AとBとどちらがいいですか。
Does not use と to list specific items
この<ruby>中<rt>なか</rt></ruby>でどれが<ruby>一番<rt>いちばん</rt></ruby><ruby>高<rt>たか</rt></ruby>い？

examples: What kind of movies do you like?
What kind of person is Tanaka?
What does this dish taste like?
What kind of place is your town?
What kind of things do you do on weekends?
What is the weather like in winter in Japan?
fields.explain:
Polite, neutral; widely used in everyday conversation.
Often combined with general nouns to open up the topic: どんな人／ところ／こと／食べ物／服.
To pin down a specific identity, do not use どんな; use どの/どれ/だれ.
“どんなの？” is natural spoken language between friends, meaning “what kind is it?”.

Asks about the “type/characteristics/nature” of a noun: a person, thing, place, or event.
Emphasizes the scope of type rather than a specific identity (unlike どの/どれ/だれ).
“どんなNでも” has an all-inclusive meaning: “any kind of … at all”.
Often used with abstract nouns:人、ところ、こと、味、色、音楽、天気、料理.
fields.notes:
“どんなに + A/V” = “no matter how …” (N3); do not confuse it with どんな + N.
To ask about quantity (how much/how long), use どのくらい/どれくらい, not どんな.
For feelings/impressions, “どんな感じ（かんじ）ですか” is very natural.
mistakes: Using どんな on its own: ×どんなが好き？ → ✓ どんな映画が好き？ or ✓何が好き？
Confusing どんな with どの/どれ when you need to choose a specific item from a list.
Confusing どんなに (higher level) with どんな + N at N5.
Using どんな to ask about quantity/duration is incorrect; use いくつ／いくら／どのくらい as appropriate.

rows: Stands alone; choose among many things
Asks about the thing itself, not its type
どのような<ruby>理由<rt>りゆう</rt></ruby>ですか。

examples: I went to school without eating breakfast.
I went out without an umbrella, so I got wet.
Please don't leave your bags here.
Don't write in kanji; please write in hiragana.
I ended up going home without saying anything.
He is studying without turning on the TV.
fields.explain:
V-ないで + V2: expresses “skipping A and doing B”, with a clear nuance of choosing an alternative.
V-ないでください: a polite request/reminder in public places and instructions.
Short spoken form: ～ないで (on its own) is used to stop someone:泣か ないで。
More formal: ～ずに (written) has an equivalent meaning in many cases.

• Meaning 1 (state/sequence): Doing the following action while skipping the preceding one (not doing V1).
• Meaning 2 (polite request/command): ～ないでください “please don't …”.
• Emphasizes alternative/contrast: “not doing A but doing B”.
• Compared with ～なくて: ～ないで focuses on “not carrying out the action”, while ～なくて usually expresses a reason/emotional result.
fields.notes:
• In clauses of cause and emotional/attitudinal results (困る、残念だ、うれしい), ～なくて is preferred.
• V-ないで + いる expresses maintaining a state of not doing something (連絡しないでいる).
• V-ないで + 済む: “not have to …” (予約したので、並ばないで済んだ).
mistakes: Confusing it with ～なくて: ×朝ご飯を食べなくて学校へ行った → 〇食べないで学校へ行った (meaning “went without eating”).
Using ないで with adjectives/nouns: ×静かないで → use ～ではなくて／～じゃなくて.
Confusing stacked negatives: ×来ないではだめ → 〇来なければだめ／来なければならない.
Forgetting to drop い in ない: ×行かないです → 〇行かないでください (for requests).
JLPT: questions often ask you to choose ないで or なくて based on the meaning “alternative” vs. “reason”.

examples: I have to submit the report by tomorrow.
You have to exercise for your health.
There are no trains, so I have to go home early.
In Japan, you have to sort your trash.
I had to attend a meeting, so I was late.
Do I have to register?
fields.explain:
Used in general requests, rules, and strong advice. Polite with いけません.
In fast conversation it can take the contracted form ないと (the rest is understood). Example: もう行かないと。
The context determines the meaning “must …”.
Used with volitional verbs/action verbs. Not used with いけない in the sense of “prohibition” (that is ～てはいけない).

• Expresses “must/have to” based on rules, circumstances, or objective needs.
• A hypothetical negative structure, “if you don't do X, it won't be OK” → implies that X must be done.
• Neutral nuance, common in conversation and ordinary writing; polite: ～ないといけません.
• Compared with ～なければならない: lighter, less compelling.
fields.notes:
• Colloquial contraction: ～ないと (with the rest omitted) often comes with an urgent intonation.
• To negate an obligation, use a double negative: 行かなくてもいい (don't have to go), not 行かないといけないの否定 directly.
• Past obligation: ～ないといけなかった states a reason/objective circumstance; polite: ～ないといけませんでした.
mistakes: Confusing it with ～てはいけない (prohibition): “入ってはいけない” = must not enter; “入らないといけない” = must enter (opposite meanings).
Wrong negation: “行かないといけない” ≠ “行ってはいけない”. Watch out for trap questions that replace と with て.
Missing いけない: “早く帰らないと” may be considered incomplete in JLPT written language, unless a conversational context allows the omission.

rows: <ruby>提出<rt>ていしゅつ</rt></ruby>しなくてはいけない
<ruby>守<rt>まも</rt></ruby>らなければならない
<ruby>勉強<rt>べんきょう</rt></ruby>しないとだめだ

examples: This document must be submitted within this week.
You must be a member to enter.
Products must be safe.
For your health, you must exercise regularly.
I have to go on a diet.
Do I have to choose from among these?
fields.explain:
Polite: change いけない → いけません to suit business/public settings.
The obligation is usually based on rules/policies; it carries little personal emotion.
To negate an obligation, use ～ なくてもいい ／～ 必要はない ; do not use いけない in a double-negative form.
In official normative documents, there is a tendency to switch to ～なければならない.

• Obligation based on rules, procedures, or general requirements: “must ...”.
• Neutral; can be used with strangers/customers in the polite form: ～なくてはいけません.
• Expresses a necessary condition: if you don't do it, it is “not OK/not allowed”.
• Focus on actions: mainly used with verbs; with A/N, used when talking about meeting a condition/standard.
fields.notes:
• Fast pronunciation: ～なくてはいけない → ～なくちゃいけない in conversation.
• Past tense for an obligation already fulfilled: ～なくてはいけなかった（had to ...）.
• Combined with other particles: どうしても行かなくてはいけない（must go no matter what）.
mistakes: Dropping “で” with N/na: ×会員なくてはいけない → 〇会員でなくてはいけない.
Sounds stiff when used for personal requests: with friends, use ～なくちゃいけない.
Wrong negation: ×行かなくてはいけないくない → 〇行かなくてもいい／行く必要はない.
Confusing it with べきだ on the exam: べきだ means “should”, not “must”.

rows: <ruby>提出<rt>ていしゅつ</rt></ruby>しなければならない。
もう<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>かなくちゃいけない。
<ruby>毎日<rt>まいにち</rt></ruby><ruby>歩<rt>ある</rt></ruby>くことだ。

fields.name: ～ね　right?
examples:
A: I work until 10 every day.
A: That must be tough.

A: Yamada's phone number is 871-6813.
B: 871-6813, right?
fields.explain: ね is used at the end of a sentence to show that the speaker expects the listener's agreement, or to confirm or remind.

examples:
A: How is this homework?
B: It's very difficult.

A: How is this town?
B: It's quiet.
fields.explain: どう： used to ask about impressions, opinions, feelings, or the nature of a thing or matter.
fields.notes:
Xはどうですか (question pattern using どう to ask about state/evaluation) means This grammar pattern is used to ask about the state, condition, or evaluation of something. It translates to 'How is X?' or 'What do you think about X?'
Structure: Xはどうですか
The phrase combines the topic particle は with どう, which means 'how' or 'in what way,' followed by ですか to form a polite question. It is commonly used to inquire about someone's opinion, condition, or the state of something in a neutral and polite manner.
